item.title: Paying for Information, Not for Clicks: A Block-Level Publisher Content Marketplace for AI Answers
item.description: arXiv:2610.30324v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a publisher content marketplace that allocates payments for information used in AI-generated answers. The unit of attribution is a ``lego block:'' a distinct fact or piece of commentary that may appear in articles from multiple publishers. A simple news-reading model connects three payment rules: equal sharing among all publishers reporting on a block, rewarding the publisher who reported a block first, and rewarding indispensable contributions. Each can be represented within a Shapley-value framework. We evaluate the framework using answers to 1,974 search-engine queries about a heavily covered news episode. When attribution considers only the articles retrieved for an individual query, most cited blocks appear unique, and the rules produce nearly identical allocations. A global index covering the full news corpus reveals overlap across publishers, making the choice of payment rule consequential. Premium publishers, defined as established outlets with substantial newsgathering operations, receive 42% of allocated value under equal sharing, compared with 46-50% under a first-publication rule, depending on the treatment of publication timestamps. These findings highlight the importance of a shared global index that records which publishers provide each block and when they published it. Attribution restricted to the sources retrieved for an individual answer lacks the information needed to distinguish these payment policies.
item.dc:creator: Markus Mobius, Luca Braghieri, Sarah Eichmeyer, Daniel G. Goldstein, Nicole Immorlica, Oliver Kiss, Ro'ee Levy, Brendan Lucier, Ishan Mahajan, Jingyi Qiu, Tanya Rosenblat, David M. Rothschild, Andras Sari, Alexsandrs Slivkins, Colin Watson

item.title: The Limits of Price Discrimination When the Market Is Unknown
item.description: arXiv:2610.30408v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Bergemann, Brooks, and Morris (2015) characterize the consumer and producer surplus pairs that segmentation can produce when the distribution of values is known. I fix only the set of possible values and characterize the pairs that some market and some segmentation can produce. They form a convex polygon. Its outer edge is the largest efficient surplus a market can have when its uniform-price profit is capped, net of that profit, and truncated equal-revenue markets attain it. At the values no segmentation is needed; strictly between two values, reaching the frontier requires splitting a market into two extremal markets. With a continuum of values up to $\bar{v}$, consumer surplus is at most $\pi\ln(\bar{v}/\pi)$ when producer surplus (the seller's profit) is $\pi$, this bound is reached without segmentation, and no market gives consumers more than $\bar{v}/e$.
item.dc:creator: Irfan Tekdir

item.title: Selling Evidence Bit by Bit
item.description: arXiv:2610.30563v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the sale of an asset to competitive buyers. Before the sale, the seller can buy hard information about the asset from an intermediary who designs and prices a test to maximize his revenue guarantee across equilibria. The test consists of one or more signals, and the seller privately chooses which subset of signals to buy and selectively discloses their realization to the buyers. We show that the intermediary benefits from splitting information into multiple signals and characterize his maximal revenue guarantee as the cumulative entropy of the asset value distribution. This guarantee is achieved by a sequence of ``skim from the top'' tests with binary, i.i.d.\ signals and additive pricing. Furthermore, any sequence of tests that achieves the maximal guarantee reveals the asset's value in the limit. For binary values, we also characterize the revenue guarantee for any given number of signals, and show that it is achieved by a test that corresponds to a ``Swiss cheese" model of failure with conclusive good news.
item.dc:creator: Nima Haghpanah, Xiao Lin, Ron Siegel

item.title: Risk Sensitivity and Stationary Equilibrium in Incomplete Markets
item.description: arXiv:2610.30956v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study stationary equilibrium and comparative statics in an incomplete market economy with risk-sensitive preferences. We prove that a stationary equilibrium exists for every nonnegative degree of risk sensitivity. With independent income, greater risk sensitivity weakly raises aggregate saving at fixed prices and weakly lowers the smallest and the largest equilibrium interest rates. With stochastically monotone Markov income, these comparisons hold when the lower risk-sensitivity parameter is sufficiently small or the upper parameter sufficiently large. For pairs of intermediate values, however, greater risk sensitivity can lower saving, contrary to an existing result in the literature, and can raise the smallest and largest equilibrium rates. An exact decomposition identifies the forces driving these reversals.
item.dc:creator: Qingyin Ma, John Stachurski, Bin Wu

item.title: A Weakly Group Strategy-Proof and Pareto-Stable Matching Mechanism with Two-Sided Indifferences under Gross Substitutes
item.description: arXiv:2610.30807v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study finite many-to-one matching markets with indifferences on both sides and publicly known firm preferences over sets of workers. A standard approach breaks ties uniformly at random and runs deferred acceptance, which is strategy-proof for workers but may select a weakly stable matching that is Pareto dominated under the agents' original preferences. For the broad class of markets in which each firm's preferences admit a gross substitutes (GS) representation, we construct a deterministic generalized deferred acceptance mechanism that is weakly stable, Pareto efficient with respect to both sides, worker weakly group strategy-proof, and implementable in strongly polynomial time given value oracles for the GS representations. This domain includes nonresponsive firm preferences, such as additive scores under matroid constraints and assignment values. Our analysis bridges ordinal matching with indifferences and competitive equilibria under imperfectly transferable utility. Although the mechanism uses only ordinal comparisons, it returns a seller-optimal equilibrium matching of a tiered auxiliary market, and the equilibrium structure of this market yields the stability, efficiency, and incentive guarantees.
item.dc:creator: Yasushi Kawase, Ryosuke Sato

item.title: A Resource Allocation Tournament
item.description: arXiv:2610.31418v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We introduce and analyze a round-robin simultaneous resource allocation contest, motivated by sports leagues and other competitive environments where agents must distribute limited resources across multiple encounters. Players allocate resources in advance to matches against all opponents, and match outcomes are determined by relative allocations. We study two payoff schemes: total points, where players accumulate rewards for each win, and winner-takes-all, where only the tournament winner is rewarded. For three players, we provide complete equilibrium characterizations under both schemes. For four or more players, we show that the total points payoff admits Blotto-type equilibria, while the winner-takes-all payoff requires numerical and algorithmic analysis. To address this, we develop a best-response dynamics algorithm with stochastic inertia and use it to approximate equilibria in games with four and five players.
item.dc:creator: Adam Nathaniel, Refael Hassin

item.title: Affirmative Action's Cumulative Fractional Assignments
item.description: arXiv:2111.11963v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: India's reservation policy entitles designated groups to fixed fractions of faculty positions. Positions are indivisible, arrive over time across departments, and appointments are irreversible. We show that no rule can keep cumulative reserved counts nondecreasing while rounding entitlements to adjacent integers at both the department and university levels; university-level compliance forces department-level errors that grow without bound. This impossibility explains why both solutions practiced in India provoked litigation and protests. A random-roster solution preserves irreversibility and department-level compliance, matches entitlements in expectation, and concentrates university-level errors. Dropping cumulative accounting restores exact rounding at both levels.
item.dc:creator: Manshu Khanna, Haydar Evren

item.title: Crowdsearch
item.description: arXiv:2311.08532v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A common economic process is crowdsearch, wherein a group of agents is invited to search for a valuable object, such as a software vulnerability or a proof-of-work nonce. We study a binary model of crowdsearch in which agents with heterogeneous search costs decide whether or not to search. Inviting more agents directly expands the pool of potential searchers, but it also increases competition for the prize and lowers individual search incentives. This crowding-out effect may dominate, so that inviting more agents can lower the probability of finding the object. We show that inviting an unlimited crowd need not guarantee success. We also provide sufficient conditions, based on the lower-tail behavior of the cost distribution, under which the probability of success is eventually increasing or eventually decreasing in the number of agents.
item.dc:creator: Hans Gersbach, Akaki Mamageishvili, Fikri Pitsuwan

item.title: Unambiguous Efficiency of Random Allocations
item.description: arXiv:2401.11899v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: When allocating indivisible objects via lottery, planners often use ordinal mechanisms, which elicit agents' rankings of objects rather than their full preferences over lotteries. In such an ordinal informational environment, planners cannot differentiate between utility profiles that induce the same ranking of objects. We propose the criterion of unambiguous efficiency: regardless of how each agent extends their preferences over objects to lotteries, the allocation is Pareto efficient with respect to the extended preferences. We compare this with the predominant efficiency criterion used for ordinal mechanisms. As an application to mechanism design, we characterize all efficient and strategy-proof mechanisms satisfying certain regularity conditions.
item.dc:creator: Eun Jeong Heo, Vikram Manjunath, Samson Alva

item.title: Limits of Disclosure in Search Markets
item.description: arXiv:2506.06319v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper examines competitive information disclosure in search markets with a mix of savvy consumers, who search costlessly, and inexperienced consumers, who face positive search costs. Savvy consumers incentivize truthful disclosure; inexperienced consumers, concealment. With both types, equilibrium features partial disclosure, which persists despite intense competition: in large markets, firms always conceal low valuations. Inexperienced consumers may search actively, but only in small markets. While savvy consumers benefit from increased competition, inexperienced consumers may be harmed. Changes in search costs have non-monotone effects: when costs are low, sufficient reductions increase informativeness and welfare; when costs are high, the opposite.
item.dc:creator: Raphael Boleslavsky, Silvana Krasteva

item.title: Moral Hazard in Delegated Bayesian Persuasion
item.description: arXiv:2604.10006v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study delegated Bayesian persuasion: a principal incentivizes an intermediary to design information via outcome-contingent transfers, while the intermediary privately chooses the experiment subject to convex costs. We characterize first-best implementability through a pair of alignment conditions on the principal's and intermediary's payoff indices. A local condition on the support of the target experiment is necessary; a global affine alignment condition is sufficient. We show that the gap between them is non-empty and provide a partial characterization of the intermediate region. When the first-best is unattainable, the principal's problem admits a virtual Bayesian persuasion representation: the second-best experiment maximizes the same concavified objective as the first-best, with the principal's payoff index distorted by a single scalar shadow price that summarizes the entire agency friction. Under entropy costs, moral hazard compresses posterior dispersion whenever the intermediary's utility differs across the actions it recommends. Explicit closed-form solutions for posteriors, mixing weights, and the optimal transfer schedule are derived for binary environments.
item.dc:creator: Wilfried Youmbi Fotso, Xun Chen, Kun Zhu

item.title: Equilibrium Architecture in Multi-Battle Contests with Count-Dependent Prizes
item.description: arXiv:2609.02031v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study how aggregating local victories shapes participation and equilibrium uniqueness. Two contestants with possibly different marginal costs compete across identical Tullock battlefields with discriminatory power at most one. A nonconstant, nondecreasing, symmetric schedule divides a fixed prize by victory count. We establish existence and show that every realized equilibrium allocation divides effort equally across battlefields. Equilibrium is unique through six battlefields, with at most two effort levels per contestant; seven first permits multiple equilibria or randomization by both contestants. The prize schedule and technology, not the cost ratio, determine whether equilibria use infinitely many effort levels; in that case, cost asymmetry changes only the higher-cost contestant's participation probability. Under majority rule, we characterize the unique equilibrium for every battlefield count and cost ratio.
item.dc:creator: Zhonghong Kuang, Jingfeng Lu

item.title: Selling to Non-linear Agents: A Demand-Based Auction
item.description: arXiv:2003.00545v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Auctions allocate scarce goods, from car licenses to online advertising, to buyers whose utilities are often not linear in money, as with budgets or risk aversion. We ask how a seller should sell to such buyers and what learning their preferences is worth. We propose demand-based auctions, which elicit demand curves and are dominant-strategy incentive compatible for any non-linear utilities. The revenue-maximizing one takes familiar second-price forms and is max-min optimal when the seller observes only demand curves. Under standard assumptions, learning risk attitudes beyond demand curves adds relatively little revenue, as does learning budgets unless they correlate with values.
item.dc:creator: Yiding Feng, Jason Hartline, Yingkai Li
